newsitem.title: UK: EMU launch expectations fell this week - JP Morgan.
newsitem.headline: EMU launch expectations fell this week - JP Morgan.

text.p: Expectations of a timely start to European economic and monetary union (EMU) in January 1999 receded in the last week, prices monitored by JP Morgan showed on Friday.

"Across the board the (probability) numbers go down by around five percent. I think that's a measure of the uncertainty caused by the bust-up between the Bundesbank and Bonn," said Avinash Persaud, head of currency research at JP Morgan.
"Underlying market sentiment...is saying there is an increased risk that EMU doesn't arrive at all, while if it does, a broad-based EMU is more likely -- expectations have moderated," he said.
The JP Morgan "EMU calculator' -- derived from the interest rate swaps market -- suggested it still saw a 100 percent chance that France and Germany would found the single currency.
But Belgium's implied probability dropped to 96 percent from 100 last Friday.
The implied probability that Spain would be in the first wave dropped to 75 percent from 80 last Friday, while Italy fell to 58 from 62 percent.
But Finland was the heaviest loser, with its chances falling to 71 percent from 79, while Ireland edged down two basis points to 73 percent and Sweden eased one point to 62 percent.
Portugal topped the list of "Club Med" hopefuls, with expectations at 79 percent compared to 83 this time last week.

Avinaush said the fact that peripheral "Club Med' hopefuls were not suffering more than more likely candidates showed there was increased risk that the single currency wouldn't happen on schedule and if did take place, it would be a broader union.

This was a result of this week's row between the German government and the Bundesbank over Bonn's plans to revalue its assets to help qualify for the single currency. If Bonn pushes the revaluation through, analysts believe there will be a soft single currency, with more members.
Only Britain and Denmark -- both of whom have a negotiated option on EMU membership -- saw a rise in assumptions they would join in 1999, according to JP Morgan's calculator.

The calculator is derived from the interest rate swaps market. The probabilities are derived from the actual swap spread, an in-house assumption of what the spread would be if EMU were not a factor, and the expected spread after EMU participation, which is zero.
The U.S. investment firm points out there is a reasonable margin of error in overall probability levels of between three and five points.
